description:
THE INCREMENTAL BLOCKER. This is the shape that stops compiler2 from staying
resident and recompiling on file change: one edit anywhere re-settles the demand
of everything.

## What is wrong

`collect_demand_cone` (jobs/runtime_demand.rs) walks transitively from the anchor
over call edges and stops only at an executable whose `RuntimeDemand` has ALREADY
settled. Driven from a cold root nothing has settled, so the walk does not stop
until it holds the entire reachable call graph, and
`produce_runtime_demand_product` settles all of them in one atomic publication.
The product key says `RuntimeDemand(E)` -- one executable -- and the unit of work
is the program.

Two numbers say it:

- `members` grows linearly with the program and reaches nearly every executable
  in it. The largest cone IS the whole program.
- `external_members` is 0 at every size. No cone ever stands on a previously
  settled one. Every settle starts cold.

## What is already right -- do not "fix" these

Measured over a ladder of n identical `Enum.find` call sites via the
`fz.compiler2.demand.cone.settled` counter (added by main d439b3acf, PR #92 --
that commit landed the MEASUREMENT for this ticket, not the fix):

- `rounds` is CONSTANT. The ascent height is a property of the lattice, not the
  program. Pinned by `the_demand_ascent_height_does_not_grow_with_the_program`.
- derivations per member is CONSTANT at ~4.8. The dirty-set skipping works.
- `cones` is CONSTANT at 4.

## RE-MEASURE BEFORE STARTING -- the input shrank ~5x

The ladder table this ticket was filed with is stale. fz-6gb landed and closed,
and it predicted exactly this: "cone size is downstream of executable count."

    n     executables (at filing -> at main 417c5b0b5)
    1     16  -> 14
    2     23  -> 17
    4     37  -> 23
    32    233 -> 45

The 231-member cone in the original table came from 233 executables; there are
now 45. Every cost figure filed with this ticket (~350ms of 3.1s at n=32,
per-settle 2.1ms -> 116.7ms, ~14% of wall clock) is against an input five times
larger than today's. Re-run the ladder first. The STRUCTURAL claim --
`external_members` = 0, cone = whole program -- is what survives unchanged and
is the actual subject.

## The obvious decomposition does NOT work

Measured with a temporary Tarjan probe over `graph.edges` (reverted):

    fixture              cone members   SCCs   largest SCC   singletons
    double+triple        7              7      1             7
    find_32 ladder       231            230    2             229

So the CALL GRAPH inside the cone is very nearly a DAG -- 229 of 230 components
are single executables, the largest genuine mutual recursion is a PAIR, and a
trivial two-function program with no recursion at all still settles as one
7-member cone.

"Decompose into call-graph SCCs and solve in reverse topological order" does not
apply, because demand does not flow one way. Per `settle_demand_cone`'s own
comment, a member's derivation reads three things:

  1. its own joined return demand   -- contributed by its CALLERS (flows down)
  2. its call-edge targets' demands -- its CALLEES (flows up)
  3. for a member producing a lambda, the input demands of every executable of
     the produced function

The demand fixpoint's dependency graph is therefore the call graph UNION its
reverse, plus lambda edges. Its SCCs are the weakly-connected components of the
call graph -- one blob, which is exactly the cone we already have. Tarjan over
call edges alone measures the wrong graph. The cone being the whole program is a
real constraint, not an oversight.

## Direction -- NOT a cone-size heuristic

Do not cap or chunk the cone. Two candidates, establish the first before
building either:

(a) STRATIFICATION. The classic two-phase demand analysis shape. If a caller's
    CONTRIBUTION to a callee's return demand depends only on the caller's own
    return demand and its body -- NOT on the caller's input demands -- then the
    two directions stratify: return demands settle top-down, then input demands
    bottom-up, with iteration needed only inside genuine call-graph SCCs
    (measured: size <= 2). `rounds` would drop toward 1 per direction. VERIFY THE
    PREMISE FIRST by reading `derive_member_demand`; item 3 above is the case
    most likely to break it, since a closure passed into a function that calls it
    is a real cycle that is not a call-graph cycle.

(b) ANCHOR ORDER. The cross-cone reuse channel ALREADY EXISTS and is threaded --
    `collect_demand_cone` stops at settled demand, `DemandGraph.external` carries
    them, `session().external_return_demand` / `external_input_demand` join
    settled outside evidence. `external_members` = 0 is therefore not a missing
    mechanism; it is an ORDERING outcome. The first `RuntimeDemand` demanded in a
    session is the root's, and from a cold root the closure swallows everything,
    so there is never an "outside" to stand on. Establish what forces root-first
    order and whether demand can be seeded from the leaves.

Note the ascent already does O(members) work per round unconditionally (the join
loop and the contributions inversion run over all members even when one member is
dirty), so rounds x whole-program is a floor no matter how good the dirty set is.

Related standing debt: fz-976 (SCC dissolution via a settled-group epoch fact),
and the note that the SCC-settled demand solver is a removal target, not a
precedent to extend.

## Checks

- `external_members` > 0 on the ladder.
- `members` for a cone anchored at a leaf executable is small.
- The flat numbers above (rounds, cones, derivations/member) stay flat.
- Full lib + matrix at baseline or better.

comments.text:
MATERIAL CORRECTION TO THIS TICKET'S DIRECTION. I filed it saying 'do not cap or chunk the cone, ask why external_members is 0'. That still holds, but I had not established WHY the cone cannot simply be decomposed, and the obvious decomposition does NOT work. Establishing this before anyone starts.

MEASURED (temporary Tarjan probe over graph.edges inside settle_demand_cone, reverted):

  fixture              cone members   SCCs   largest SCC   singletons
  double+triple        7              7      1             7
  find_32 ladder       231            230    2             229

So the CALL GRAPH inside a 231-member cone is very nearly a DAG: 229 of 230 components are single executables and the largest genuine mutual recursion is a PAIR. The cone is not one big knot of recursion. A trivial two-function program (double, triple -- no call between them, no recursion anywhere) still settles as one 7-member cone with 7 singleton components.

WHY THE OBVIOUS FIX IS WRONG. 'Decompose the cone into call-graph SCCs and solve in reverse topological order' does not apply, because demand does not flow one way. Per settle_demand_cone's own comment (jobs/runtime_demand.rs ~line 585), a member's derivation reads exactly three things:
  1. its own joined return demand   -- contributed by its CALLERS (flows down)
  2. its call-edge targets' demands -- its CALLEES (flows up)
  3. for a member producing a lambda, the input demands of every executable of the produced function
So the demand fixpoint's dependency graph is the call graph UNION its reverse (plus lambda edges). Its SCCs are the weakly-connected components of the call graph -- one blob -- which is exactly the cone we already have. Tarjan over call edges alone measures the wrong graph for this purpose. That is why the cone is the whole program, and it is a real constraint, not an oversight.

WHAT THAT LEAVES, in order of what to establish first:

(a) STRATIFICATION. This is the classic two-phase demand analysis shape. If a caller's CONTRIBUTION to a callee's return demand depends only on the caller's own return demand and its body -- NOT on the caller's input demands -- then the two directions stratify: return demands settle top-down over the call graph, then input demands settle bottom-up, with iteration needed only inside genuine call-graph SCCs (measured above: size <= 2). rounds would drop from 14 (which currently looks like graph DEPTH, since information moves one hop per round) toward 1 per direction. VERIFY THE PREMISE FIRST by reading derive_member_demand; item 3 above (lambda capture demands) is the case most likely to break it, since a closure passed into a function that calls it is a real cycle that is not a call-graph cycle.

(b) ANCHOR ORDER. The cross-cone reuse channel ALREADY EXISTS and is already threaded -- collect_demand_cone stops at an executable whose demand has settled, DemandGraph.external carries them, and session().external_return_demand / external_input_demand join settled outside evidence. external_members = 0 is therefore not a missing mechanism; it is an ORDERING outcome. The first RuntimeDemand demanded in a session is the root's, and from a cold root the closure swallows everything, so there is never an 'outside' to stand on. If leaf executables settled first, later cones would stop at them. Establish what forces the root-first order and whether anything prevents seeding demand from the leaves.

(b) is the cheaper experiment and does not require (a) to be true. Do it first.

DO NOT infer from rounds=14 that the ascent is inefficient -- it is constant across a 32x ladder and is pinned by the_demand_ascent_height_does_not_grow_with_the_program. 14 is the price of moving information one hop per round across a graph that deep; ordering the work is what removes it, not tuning the ascent.

HYPOTHESES TESTED BEFORE IMPLEMENTING. Both directions I proposed in the previous comment were checked experimentally. THE STRATIFICATION DIRECTION IS DEAD; the ordering direction is untested-by-natural-data and carries a risk I had not identified. All probes reverted; nothing in this comment is speculation.

METHOD. A differential probe inside the Jacobi ascent: after each real derive_member_demand, re-derive the SAME member against a copy of the round's reads with only that member's OWN input demands perturbed, and compare the contributions it produces for its callees. If contributions never move, the caller->callee flow is independent of the caller's input side and the two directions stratify.

H2: 'a caller's contribution to its callee is independent of the caller's own input demands' -- FALSIFIED.
  enum_take_drop_split   12 of 6666 derivations changed
  enum_map_family        48 of 3540
  enum_sort               2 of 108
  enum_predicate_search   0 of 6800
  quicksort               0 of 20
  enum_tier0              0 of 520
Rare (0.18% on the worst fixture) and absent on half the corpus, but real. Two-phase 'return demands top-down, then input demands bottom-up' is NOT SOUND as stated.

Three follow-up hypotheses about WHICH coupling this is -- ALL THREE FALSIFIED, recording them so nobody re-runs them:

- 'The violators are lambda producers' (the case the ascent's own comment flags, item 3: a member producing a lambda reads the produced function's input demands). FALSE. 0 of the violating members produce a callable. Violators are count/2, map_every_list/4, scan_list/3, with_index_list/2, with_index_list/3, sort_list/2 -- recursive list walkers with an accumulator.
- 'The coupling is on the CALLABLE axis (a callable passed through as an input)'. FALSE, and the reverse is true. RuntimeDemand is { shape, callable }; perturbing each axis alone:
      SHAPE axis:    12 / 48 / 2 changes on the three affected fixtures
      CALLABLE axis:  0 changes on EVERY fixture (2918 / 1618 / 28 / 2808 perturbations)
  NOTE A METHOD ERROR WORTH AVOIDING: RuntimeDemand::whole() sets shape=Whole AND resets callable to default, so a first pass using it perturbed both axes at once and pointed at the wrong one. Perturb one axis at a time.
- 'The coupling is confined to a recursion cycle, so it stays inside a call-graph SCC and stratification survives across SCCs'. FALSE. Every changed edge goes to an ordinary downstream callee with self=false and mutual=false: count/2 -> +/2, with_index_list/3 -> +/2, sort_list/2 -> reverse_list/1, scan_list/3 -> two lambdas.

WHAT THE COUPLING ACTUALLY IS (mechanism, from the code): contributions carry input_demands as well as return_demand, and they are persisted through replace_settled_input_demand_contributions -- a caller PINNING positions on its callee's inputs. So input demand does not flow purely bottom-up; a caller contributes downward to its callee's input side, and what it contributes depends on its own input demands. That is the second bidirectional edge, and it is why the cone is the whole program. It is NOT intrinsic to demand analysis -- half the corpus never exercises it -- so characterizing that channel narrowly is the real lead, not stratification.

H1 (ordering): NOT CONFIRMED, and riskier than I wrote. Natural data never exercises the reuse channel -- probe shows already_settled_in_cone=0 for every cone on every fixture, i.e. the earlier small cones are DISJOINT from the big one, so nothing was ever available to stand on. The mechanism does exist (collect_demand_cone reads runtime demand for non-anchor members and files them as external). But settling a callee BEFORE its callers have contributed settles it with no caller evidence, and the caller's later contribution displaces and re-settles it -- the stale-caller window the producer already handles by re-collecting. So bottom-up ordering trades scope for CHURN.

CHURN BASELINE, measure any decomposition against it: today it is ZERO. find_8 publishes 65 member-settlements for 65 executables; enum_take_drop_split publishes 278 for 278. Every executable's demand settles EXACTLY ONCE. The current design buys that with scope -- one cone, no re-settling. Any decomposition must beat scope without paying it back in re-settles.

RECOMMENDED NEXT STEP, changed from the previous comment: do not start on either direction. Characterize the caller-pins-callee-input channel first -- why a caller must pin its callee's input positions at all, whether that pin is derivable from something already settled (transport/ABI facts look like the natural owner), and what the 0.18% of edges that use it have in common. If that channel can be sourced from elsewhere, input demand becomes bottom-up-only and stratification comes back with it.

COMPLETE CHARACTERIZATION. Seven hypotheses tested by differential probing inside the ascent (perturb one input to a real derivation, re-derive, diff the output). All probes reverted; tree clean; both guard tests green. THIS SUPERSEDES MY EARLIER COMMENT SAYING STRATIFICATION IS DEAD -- that conclusion was drawn from a test that asked the wrong question.

=== THE COUPLING MAP (what depends on what) ===

Write IN(X) for X's input demands, RET(X) for its return demand, and C(M->X) for what M contributes to callee X.

1. C(M->X) vs M's OWN input demands: coupled ONLY when M is inside a call-graph cycle.
     members IN a cycle:   2489 perturbations,  62 violations
     members NOT in a cycle: 15390 perturbations,  0 violations   (7 fixtures)
   Every violator is self-recursive, 100%: count/2, map_every_list/4, scan_list/3, with_index_list/2, with_index_list/3, sort_list/2. Mechanism, from List.count/2:
     fnp count([], acc), do: acc
     fnp count([_head | tail], acc), do: count(tail, acc + 1)
   The target is +/2. What count/2 demands of +/2's RESULT is the demand on the value it passes to its own recursive call at slot 1 -- i.e. count/2's own IN slot 1. Recursion is what makes IN and RET mutually dependent, and it is the ONLY thing that does.

2. C(M->X) vs X's OWN input demands: NEVER coupled. 21089 per-callee perturbations across 4 fixtures, return_to_THAT_callee_moved = 0 in every single one. THERE IS NO 2-CYCLE ACROSS A CALL EDGE. This is the load-bearing negative result.

3. C(M->X) vs X's SIBLING callees' input demands: coupled, ~16% of per-callee perturbations. This is the within-body data-flow chain -- in f(g(x)), what you demand of g's result IS f's input demand at that slot. Acyclic within a body (values are defined before use), so it orders, it does not iterate.

4. IN(X) vs RET(X): coupled, 3-11% of derivations. Expected -- liveness flows backward from the output.

5. Which HALF of the contribution moves under (1): return_demand ONLY. changed_input_only = 0 and changed_both = 0 on every fixture. The caller-pins-callee-input channel (callable_boundary_input_demand_contributions_product) is NOT a source of coupling -- I had guessed it was, wrongly.

6. Axis: SHAPE only. Perturbing the CALLABLE axis alone changed contributions 0 times on every fixture (7000+ perturbations). METHOD WARNING: RuntimeDemand::whole() sets shape=Whole AND resets callable to default, so a probe using it moves both axes and points at the wrong one. Perturb one axis at a time.

=== WHAT THIS MEANS ===

The demand system's ONLY genuine fixpoints are call-graph cycles. Everything else is a DAG of dependencies that an evaluation ORDER would settle in one pass instead of 14 rounds.

And the cycles are tiny and rare (Tarjan over cone call edges, self-loops counted separately -- note Tarjan reports a self-recursive node as a SINGLETON, so self-loops must be counted or you will conclude the graph is acyclic when it is not):
    enum_take_drop_split   276 members,   3 self-recursive, largest mutual SCC 2
    enum_map_family        155 members,  14 self-recursive
    enum_sort               27 members,   4 self-recursive
    find_32 ladder         231 members, 230 SCCs, largest 2

So a 231-member x 14-round monolith is standing in for ~230 single-node evaluations plus 3-4 two-node fixpoints.

Suggestive, not conclusive: members SHALLOW in the call graph settle LAST (last-changed round 12-15) while deep members settle early (rounds 3-8), consistent with the 14 rounds being upward percolation of input demand one hop per round -- i.e. ordering waste, not real iteration. The depth metric used saturates through cycles (reported d551 on a 276-member graph), so re-measure with proper SCC condensation before relying on it.

=== THE REMAINING DESIGN QUESTION ===

Not 'can it be decomposed' -- it can. It is 'what is the order', and the measurements constrain it sharply without settling it: RET(X) needs its CALLERS, IN(X) needs its CALLEES, and IN(X) needs RET(X). Those pull in opposite directions, so a naive single topological sweep does not obviously suffice. Establish whether a static order exists over the SCC-condensed graph or whether a bounded local iteration per SCC neighbourhood is needed.

=== THE CONSTRAINT ANY DESIGN MUST MEET ===

Churn is ZERO today: find_8 publishes 65 member-settlements for 65 executables, enum_take_drop_split 278 for 278. Every executable's demand settles EXACTLY ONCE. The current design buys that with scope. A decomposition that settles an SCC before its callers have contributed will settle it at ignore and then displace and re-settle it -- the stale-caller window the producer already handles by re-collecting. Beat scope WITHOUT paying it back in re-settles, and measure both.

DEPRIORITIZED BEHIND fz-6gb. Do not start this ticket first.

Measured the absolute cost this ticket is a share of, and it is a small share. On enum_predicate_search the demand cone is ~350ms of 2.69s -- about 13%. Meanwhile fz-6gb (each distinct lambda literal drags a private copy of every shared library function it reaches) is worth 9.2x wall clock on a 32-call-site program.

More to the point, fz-6gb SHRINKS THIS TICKET'S PROBLEM. Cone size is downstream of executable count, and the three-way control in fz-6gb shows it directly:
  32 distinct lambdas   233 executables   231 cone members
  32 identical lambdas  233 executables   231 cone members
  1 shared lambda        16 executables    14 cone members
The whole-program cone this ticket is about is 231 members largely BECAUSE there are 233 executables where ~47 would do. Fixing the cone first means engineering against an input 15x larger than it needs to be, and every measurement recorded here -- members, rounds, derivations, the SCC census -- would have to be retaken afterwards anyway.

Everything established here stays valid and is worth keeping: the coupling map, the proof that there is no 2-cycle across a call edge (0 of 21089 per-callee perturbations), that coupling occurs only inside call-graph cycles (0 of 15390 acyclic perturbations), and that churn is currently zero. Re-measure the SIZES after fz-6gb; the STRUCTURE will not have changed.

STAYS OPEN, and the commit that carries this ticket's name landed only half of it.

`fz-zg4: make the demand cone's cost visible in telemetry` (main d439b3acf, PR
#92) added the `fz.compiler2.demand.cone.settled` counter and the
`the_demand_ascent_height_does_not_grow_with_the_program` pin. That is the
MEASUREMENT this ticket needed, not the fix. None of this ticket's Checks are
met:

    external_members > 0 on the ladder                       NOT MET
    members for a cone anchored at a leaf is small           NOT MET
    the flat numbers stay flat                               holds
    lib + matrix at baseline                                 holds

Anyone reading `git log` should not take the commit prefix as closure.

RE-MEASURE BEFORE STARTING. fz-6gb has landed and closed, and it predicted this
ticket's input would shrink: "cone size is downstream of executable count". It
was right. The 32-site ladder that produced the 231-member cone in this ticket's
table now compiles to 45 executables, not 233:

    n     executables (was -> now)
    1     16  -> 14
    2     23  -> 17
    4     37  -> 23
    32    233 -> 45

So the measured ladder in this description is against an input ~5x larger than
today's. Re-run it before designing anything -- the cost figures (~350ms of 3.1s
at n=32, per-settle 2.1ms -> 116.7ms) are stale, and the structural question
("why must a cone be collected cold at all -- external_members = 0 is an
ORDERING outcome, not a missing mechanism") is the part that survives unchanged.

The 2026-08-23 correction on this ticket -- that the demand fixpoint's dependency
graph is the call graph UNION its reverse, so call-graph SCC decomposition
measures the wrong graph -- also still stands and is the most valuable thing
here. Read it first.

title: RuntimeDemand is keyed per executable but computed per program: the demand cone spans the whole reachable call graph and never reuses a settled one
